title: Better Apart: When a Carve-Out Transforms Both Companies

Carve-outs often achieve a clean separation but leave much of the deal’s value unrealized. BCG argues that companies should use the disruption to redesign both the divested business and the remaining company—an approach associated with materially stronger shareholder returns.

Transformation delivers more value than separation aloneCarve-outs paired with a comprehensive transformation agenda outperform conventional separations by 20.3 percentage points of total shareholder return, because they reset strategy and operating models rather than merely preserve continuity.

Remainco is the overlooked test of whether the deal workedPrograms often give NewCo the resources to stand alone while treating RemainCo as a cleanup exercise. Yet RemainCo more often underperforms after close, exposing the cost of leaving its strategy unchanged.

Leaders must move through three layers of ambitionSeparation establishes day-one viability; rationalization removes duplication and stranded costs; transformation redesigns how each business competes. Many programs stop at the first 2 layers, optimizing an inherited model instead of creating superior ones.

Early, CEO-backed governance protects the full-potential agendaA transformation and separation office should integrate deal milestones with strategic choices before they become locked in. It needs protected senior capacity and CEO authority to ensure both companies launch with distinct, future-ready designs.

Most carve-outs achieve separation. Some go further by realizing efficiencies. Far fewer capture the maximum value the transaction makes possible. Companies that pair carve-outs with a comprehensive transformation agenda outperform those that rely on conventional separation approaches by 20.3 percentage points of total shareholder return. (See Exhibit 1.) 

The gap reflects differences in both ambition and scope. Carve-out programs are typically organized around a narrow mandate: separate cleanly, minimize disruption, stand up NewCo, address stranded costs, and move on. Those activities are essential, but they do not answer the more consequential question: How should NewCo and RemainCo each be redesigned for the markets they will compete in, the customers and investors they will serve, and the cost structures, capabilities, and strategic priorities they will carry forward?A full-potential carve-out begins with that question. It treats separation as a catalyst for transformation: an opportunity to design two future-ready companies from a clean slate, rather than simply divide the inherited enterprise into two distinct operating units. The goal is not to produce separate versions of the old model. It is to build two reimagined businesses with operating models, cost structures, capabilities, and management systems reset and tailored to the realities each will face after separation.Rethinking the Carve-Out Opportunity
When success is defined primarily as Day 1 readiness, continuity naturally becomes the program’s priority. NewCo receives leadership attention, readiness milestones, capability build-out, talent transfers, and a plan for operating independently. RemainCo often receives a narrower agenda: remove stranded costs, eliminate duplication, exit transition service agreements (TSAs), and rationalize roles and processes.The result is an imbalance. RemainCo is treated literally as what remains after the asset is gone, rather than as a future company requiring a new strategy, ambition, operating model, organizational structure, culture, and investor story.Post-close performance consistently reflects that divergence, with RemainCo the more frequent underperformer relative to NewCo across comparable transactions. (See Exhibit 2.)

That makes RemainCo’s performance a critical test of whether a carve-out has been transformational or executed mechanically. Its leaders must confront questions that conventional separation programs often defer: What should the company become once the asset is gone? Who are its relevant peers? Where should it compete? Which capabilities should it own, build, outsource, automate, or discontinue? What new strategy, priorities, leadership, incentives, investments, and cultural signals will make it feel like a focused new enterprise?The opportunity extends well beyond cost reduction. A carve-out releases capital, refocuses management attention, and creates an opening to redesign both companies. Leaders can reconsider strategic focus, organizational structure, spans of control, geographic footprint, decision rights, shared services, incentives, culture, and the technology and data foundation of each business.The specific choices will vary by industry. A consumer-products or retail company might reset brand investment, channel roles, pricing, and revenue-growth management. An industrial or automotive company might simplify product platforms, reshape its manufacturing footprint, strengthen procurement, or redesign operations around a more focused portfolio.

A carve-out releases capital, refocuses management attention, and creates an opening to redesign both companies.

This opportunity is also time-sensitive. Before Day 1, teams are disentangling systems, reworking processes, reallocating talent, redefining governance, and resetting leadership roles. Fundamental design choices can be incorporated in tandem while the organization is already in flux. After Day 1, those choices tend to become more difficult, more political, and more expensive.Not every element of transformation must be completed by Day 1. But the strategic direction, target operating models, critical leadership choices, and transformation roadmap should be established before it. Day 1 should mark both operational independence and the launch of new, fit-for-purpose future companies. Legacy obligations such as TSAs and residual disentanglement may continue, but they should not define either company’s trajectory.The Three Layers of Value Creation
A carve-out program can be designed around one of three layers, each reflecting a different level of ambition: separation, rationalization, or transformation. (See Exhibit 3.) A full-potential carve-out targets the transformation layer while delivering the requirements of the two layers beneath it.

This value stack helps leaders distinguish activity from ambition. The same workstreams—impacting areas including technology, organization, processes, contracts, and people—appear at every layer. What distinguishes the layers are the ambition and scope behind the work.Separation: Establishing Viability. At the separation layer, the objective is to ensure that both companies can operate independently from Day 1. The work includes disentangling systems, defining TSAs, standing up essential functions, allocating assets and people, and protecting business continuity. The governing question is: Can both companies operate safely and independently?The measure of success is viability. This work is essential, but it does not by itself create a better business.Rationalization: Improving the Inherited Model. At the rationalization layer, the objective shifts from viability to efficiency. The program removes stranded costs and duplication, right-sizes support functions, rationalizes the footprint, exits TSAs, and eliminates processes that existed only because of the former corporate perimeter. The governing question is: Can both companies operate more efficiently within the model they inherited?These actions can produce substantial value. But rationalization optimizes the inherited model; it does not determine whether that model remains the right one. It does not reset strategic ambition, fundamentally change governance, or create the capabilities and culture required for a different level of performance.This is where many carve-out programs stop. The businesses have been separated, costs have been removed, and inherited complexity has been reduced. The transaction may be considered complete even though its broader potential remains unrealized.

Rationalization optimizes the inherited model; it does not determine whether that model remains the right one.

Transformation: Designing the Model Required to Outperform. At the transformation layer, leaders ask a more fundamental question: How should each company be redesigned to compete and outperform on its own?That question opens three interconnected agendas:Strategic Ambition. Leaders determine where each business will play after separation, how it will win, and what level of performance it should target outside the constraints of the former perimeter. For RemainCo, this begins with identifying its future peers and defining best-in-class performance for a company of its new size, scope, and strategic position. Realizing that ambition may require a sharper portfolio, different capital allocation, fewer geographies, a new role for corporate functions, and/or a more compelling investor narrative. For NewCo, it may mean a more focused go-to-market model, a higher growth ambition, or distinctive standalone capabilities. Operating-Model and Capability Redesign. Leaders determine how each company should be structured, governed, and enabled. This goes beyond lifting and shifting the inherited model while removing duplication. Leaders must ask what the organization should look like, how it should operate, what new talent may be required, and which inherited elements—if any—should continue to exist or be replaced. Answering those questions requires leaders to reconsider decision rights, roles, processes, organizational layers, technology, data, and the balance among owned, shared, outsourced, and automated capabilities. NewCo may be able to build modern, fit-for-purpose systems without reproducing the parent’s legacy environment. RemainCo may have an equally valuable opportunity to simplify its technology base, redirect investment, and align its capabilities with a more focused portfolio. Leadership, People, and Culture Activation. Leadership teams should be selected to meet the needs and aspirations of the future companies, not simply carried over from the legacy organization. Incentives must reinforce the new performance agenda, and employees must understand how the new model will change their day-to-day work. Management routines, leadership behavior, and visible cultural signals should demonstrate that Day 1 is not merely an administrative milestone but the launch of a comprehensive business transformation. Without culture activation at the heart of the effort, strategy and operating-model choices remain designs on paper. A reset culture and change agenda that mobilizes and inspires people can foster the new mindsets and behaviors needed to propel the organization forward.

Treating NewCo as the transformation opportunity while assigning RemainCo only a separation-and-cleanup agenda is insufficient and leaves value unrealized.

Transformation will not look the same on both sides of the transaction. NewCo and RemainCo will operate in different contexts, face different competitors, and have different capital, capability, and competitive requirements. Treating NewCo as the transformation opportunity while assigning RemainCo only a separation-and-cleanup agenda is insufficient and leaves value unrealized.Leading carve-outs transform both entities at the same time. (See “When Separation Becomes Transformation.”)

When Separation Becomes Transformation

Two transactions—one centered on reshaping RemainCo, the other on creating distinct agendas for both RemainCo and NewCo—show how separation can become a platform for transformation.A Mining Group Rebuilds RemainCo Around a Focused PortfolioA global mining group announced a radical portfolio simplification in the early 2020s, divesting multiple businesses in a sequenced multiyear program, to refocus the continuing company on its core. The case is instructive precisely because the separation agenda was framed not just as a series of carve-outs but as the redesign of the continuing core company. Each transaction was sequenced to deliver the future portfolio, the future capital structure, the future cost base, and the future leadership and operating model the continuing company would need to compete against a narrower and more focused peer set. The continuing company became not what was left behind; it represented what was being built.An Automaker Builds Two Businesses for Different MarketsIn one automotive separation, the parent company used the carve-out to create two businesses with fundamentally different customer groups, product cycles, technology transitions, capital needs, and investor expectations. The remaining business sharpened its focus on premium passenger vehicles, electrification, software, and brand economics. The separated business gained independence to pursue commercial vehicles, fleet customers, industrial performance, uptime, total cost of ownership, and zero-emission transport.The separation did more than create two legal entities. It allowed each business to be governed, funded, benchmarked, and managed against the economics of its own market rather than constrained by a shared corporate structure. The full-potential lesson is that the value of the carve-out came not only from separation, but also from designing two more coherent businesses with distinct strategic agendas.

Transformation, then, makes a different set of choices about how each business will compete, operate, invest, and mobilize. A practical test is whether the program can clear three gates:Framing. Is the transaction explicitly framed as a transformation, with a clear view of what each newly independent company can deliver for stakeholders—and of the strategy, performance ambition, operational, capability, and people-related choices needed to realize that potential?Symmetry. Are NewCo and RemainCo each being redesigned with equal ambition—including what each should stop, start, rethink, or reallocate now that the perimeter has shifted?Structure. Is a dedicated, CEO-backed program structure in place with the authority and capacity to make critical decisions early, translate them into action, and sustain the transformation beyond Day 1?If the program cannot clear all three gates, it is still managing separation and rationalization. It is not yet managing transformation.Designing for Full Potential
A full-potential carve-out needs a program capable of running all levels of the value stack simultaneously. Three choices shape whether it succeeds: scope, timing, and program structure. (See Exhibit 4.)

Scope establishes a broad enough ambition, and timing allows that ambition to influence critical decisions at the best moment. Program structure—the governance, capacity, and leadership mechanisms that translate the right ambition and its optimal timing into sustained and meaningful action—requires strong, dedicated support. Without it, even the right choices made at the right time can be overwhelmed by the demands of separation and business as usual. Together, the three determine whether a carve-out produces merely two independent companies—or two much stronger ones.Scope. A conventional carve-out asks how to replicate the existing business in standalone form as cleanly and safely as possible. A full-potential carve-out asks how NewCo and RemainCo should each be redesigned to succeed on their own terms. Narrow scope preserves the inherited model. Broader scope asks whether functions should be redesigned, automated, or sourced differently; whether AI and digital workflows can replace inherited work; and whether the product, customer, or geographic perimeter should change now that the constraints of the former portfolio have been removed.Timing. Decisions that create value must be made early enough to shape the separation agenda, rather than retrofitted after close, when separation actions may already have locked in choices that limit value creation. TSA design can constrain future systems choices. Leaving governance and operating model design unchanged can reinforce suboptimal decision rights. Mechanical—rather than strategic—organizational design, role definition, and leadership appointments can stymie culture activation and the change ambition. Considered early, these choices can make transformation an outcome of separation. Made too late, they can reinforce the inherited status quo and make transformation impossible.Not every transformation initiative must be completed before Day 1. But the strategy, value roadmap, future operating model, people choices, and target culture should be established early enough to influence separation decisions. Leaders should distinguish between choices that must be made before Day 1, capabilities required on Day 1, and transformation initiatives that will continue after Day 1 as the companies complete their transition to fully independent operations.

Leaders should distinguish between choices that must be made before Day 1, capabilities required on Day 1, and transformation initiatives that will continue after Day 1.

Program Structure. A carve-out inevitably touches the elements that shape each future company: leadership, governance, systems, processes, and ways of working. The issue is not whether these elements will be reconsidered; the carve-out already puts them in play. It is whether decisions about them will be made through a narrow separation lens or through the broader lens of company transformation.Applying a transformation lens requires protected capacity with CEO-level backing: a small, credible, cross-functional team of senior leaders. The team must be close enough to the businesses to sustain implementation yet sufficiently protected to keep transformation from being crowded out by separation or business as usual. Its composition should reflect the value thesis. An industrial carve-out may need manufacturing, procurement, engineering, and supply-chain leaders at its center. A health care carve-out may require regulatory, quality, medical, and commercial leaders. A technology carve-out may depend most heavily on product, architecture, data, and talent leaders.The organizational mechanism that provides this protected capacity is a transformation and separation office (TSO). It is not simply a conventional separation management office (SMO) with a longer task list. A conventional SMO focuses on ensuring that both businesses can operate independently on Day 1. The TSO goes further: it addresses the choices that must be made before Day 1 and the transformation initiatives needed thereafter to help both businesses achieve and sustain their new ambitions.The TSO has four jobs. First, it integrates separation milestones with the value agenda, so that choices about governance, operations, organization, people, and technology advance the transformation ambition—not only business continuity and simplification mandates. Second, it establishes a clear prioritization framework for making strategic and operational tradeoffs while they can still shape the future models. Third, it protects the transformation agenda from the immediate demands of separation and sustains it beyond Day 1. Fourth, it mobilizes leaders and the broader organization around the new ambition and the mindsets and behaviors each company will need to thrive.The TSO must therefore be designed around outcomes rather than process. It should translate the strategy and value thesis into initiatives with clear goals, owners, milestones, and business cases; link operating-model choices to financial targets and KPIs; align incentives to outcomes; and manage residual separation requirements without allowing them to define the future businesses. It should also equip leaders to tell a consistent change story to investors, customers, employees, and partners.Just as important, the TSO must establish and pursue an equally ambitious transformation agenda for RemainCo. A compelling NewCo transformation still fails to realize the carve-out’s maximum potential if the continuing company emerges operationally intact but strategically unchanged.

A compelling NewCo transformation still fails to realize the carve-out’s maximum potential if the continuing company emerges operationally intact but strategically unchanged.

The TSO needs a dedicated senior leader—either an internal executive relieved of existing responsibilities or an external hire—with full and visible CEO backing. When tradeoffs become difficult, the CEO must hold leaders across the organization accountable for both Day 1 readiness and transformation, insist that decisions remain aligned with the strategic priorities set by the transformation agenda, and ensure that the urgency of separation does not crowd out the work required to create long-term value.

The objective of a full-potential carve-out is not merely Day 1 readiness. It is to use separation as a clean-slate moment to design and build both companies for what comes next. That opportunity is rare: a carve-out is a major change event and often a once-in-a-generation opening. Internally, the business is being redesigned, and employees are anticipating a new chapter. Externally, customers, competitors, and investors are reassessing each company and its prospects. Used narrowly, a carve-out produces a clean split. Used to its full potential, it creates a clean slate, with two companies deliberately built to outperform on their own.
